Photograph the lesion and defer all description — type, colour, texture, border, size, distribution and evolution — until the dermatology referral has been accepted
Description is the first step, not something deferred.
Biopsy every pigmented lesion before any description of type, colour, texture, border or evolution, since morphology is unreliable in premalignant disease
Biopsy is triggered by concerning features, not used in place of describing.
Characterise it systematically — primary lesion type, colour, surface texture, border definition, size, distribution, palpability, ulceration, bleeding, induration and temporal evolution

Sharp demarcation with thick silvery scale, and rapid complete response to a topical corticosteroid

Malignant T cells migrating into the skin over years, arising in the lymphoid tissue

Human herpesvirus 8 combined with a weakened immune system, arising in the cells lining blood and lymph vessels

At least annual skin examination alone, with lymph nodes assessed only once metastasis is suspected clinically

New or changing single-digit longitudinal melanonychia, proximal widening, Hutchinson sign, or nail dystrophy with pigment

Longitudinal pigmented bands present in several nails since childhood, unchanged in width, colour, thickness and spacing over many years, with no nail dystrophy

Any nail change at all in a patient over 65, and any nail that has been abnormal for more than a month, whatever the appearance or the number of digits involved

When the lesion has recurred twice after cryotherapy; radiation therapy, hedgehog pathway inhibitors, programmed death 1 blockade, and cetuximab as a possible benefit

Usually rapidly growing and rarely curable even when treated early; morbidity comes chiefly from early distant metastasis to lung and liver, with local destruction uncommon

Usually slow-growing and highly curable when treated early; morbidity comes chiefly from nodal metastasis, which occurs in 3 to 7% of cases, rather than from local destruction

No specific education is needed once the lesions have been treated successfully, since the surrounding field carries no further risk and reactions to therapy are not expected
The field remains at risk, so education continues.

Daily broad-spectrum sun protection and protective clothing; expect local treatment reactions such as erythema and crusting and adhere to the field therapy duration; seek prompt review of any non-healing or changing lesion

Sun protection in the summer months only and no protective clothing; expect no local reaction to field treatment; return only if an entirely new lesion appears

Rough sandpaper papules on sun-exposed skin, usually under 6 mm; it may resemble seborrheic keratosis
Those are actinic keratosis features.
Localised or generalised erythematous patches or scaly plaques, usually on the trunk and frequently larger than 5 cm; it may resemble psoriasis, eczema or tinea
Correct — which is why diagnosis is often delayed.

set2.q: At what Breslow thickness is sentinel lymph node biopsy offered or discussed, and what lowers that threshold?
opts: At 0.8 mm or greater; or at 1.0 mm or greater when additional histologic risk factors are present — ulceration, high mitotic rate, or lymphovascular invasion
The two thresholds are the wrong way round.
At 4.0 mm or greater; or at 2.0 mm or greater when additional histologic risk factors are present — ulceration or high mitotic rate
Both thresholds are far higher than the deck gives.
At any thickness once the diagnosis is confirmed, since thickness does not influence the decision to stage the nodes
Thickness is precisely what drives the decision.
At 1.0 mm or greater; or at 0.8 mm or greater when additional histologic risk factors are present — ulceration, high mitotic rate, or lymphovascular invasion
Correct — three risk factors lower the threshold.
